story_ideas.title: BLS: Nursing care facilities employment, August 2026 — 1,590.20 thousands of jobs (+2.1% year over year)
story_ideas.headline: Nursing homes added workers this year, just not many
story_ideas.angle: The August 2026 nursing care facilities employment level of 1,590.20 thousands of jobs, up 2.1%, read by families judging whether a facility can staff its shifts.
story_ideas.hook: Monitored publishers cover this beat and none has matched the August figure, making it a live opportunity.
story_ideas.consumer: When you tour a facility, ask how many open positions it is carrying on each shift and how often it uses agency staff, then compare that answer to the staffing measures on its CMS profile.
story_ideas.b2b: A 2.1% annual gain sets the ceiling on census growth and on any staffing ratio an operator promises a referral source.
story_ideas.why: If the building you are considering cannot fill shifts, the quality measures you are reading were produced under conditions that may not last.
story_ideas.note: National figure with facility-level CMS staffing data available for state and county comparison.

story_ideas.title: BLS: Home health care services employment, August 2026 — 1,896.40 thousands of jobs (+5.0% year over year)
story_ideas.headline: There are now more home health workers than nursing home workers, and the gap is widening
story_ideas.angle: Home health employment at 1,896.40 thousands of jobs, up 5.0% year over year, for older adults deciding whether care at home is realistically staffable where they live.
story_ideas.hook: Home health grew at more than twice the rate of nursing care facilities over the same year.
story_ideas.consumer: If you are planning to stay in your home, this is the year to ask agencies about their current caseload and wait times rather than assuming availability later.
story_ideas.b2b: Home health is absorbing the same labor pool facilities are recruiting from, which reprices agency contracts and turnover assumptions.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Penalties
story_ideas.headline: The fines your nursing home paid are public again

story_ideas.hook: A refreshed public file that lets anyone put a dollar figure on three years of enforcement at a specific address.
story_ideas.consumer: Look up every facility on your list and note whether it has payment denials as well as fines, then ask the administrator what changed afterward.
story_ideas.b2b: Enforcement history follows a building through referrals and admissions, and operators should know what a family sees before the tour.
story_ideas.why: A fine record you never checked is the one piece of a facility's history nobody will volunteer.
story_ideas.note: Refreshed reference file, not an event; state and county breakouts supported.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Health Deficiencies
story_ideas.headline: Three years of nursing home citations, one row at a time
story_ideas.angle: The health citation file with citation tag, scope and severity, current status and correction date, for anyone trying to tell a paperwork violation from a care failure.
story_ideas.hook: Scope and severity, not citation counts, is what separates a clerical finding from harm, and both are in the file.

story_ideas.b2b: Citation patterns by tag are the clearest signal of where survey readiness is failing across a portfolio.

feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** The long-term care evidence holds together this run across four sources, and what it shows is a nursing home being judged on staffing in a labor market that is pulling workers toward the front door. The CMS provider files refreshed 08/01/26 include Provider Information, which carries the certified bed counts, staffing and quality scores used in the Five-Star Rating System, alongside Health Deficiencies, Penalties, Ownership and Survey Summary, each covering the last three years of citations, fines and inspections. Set against those facility-level records, BLS puts nursing care facilities employment at 1,590.20 thousands of jobs in August 2026, up 2.1% year over year, while home health care services employment reached 1,896.40 thousands of jobs, up 5.0%, at average hourly earnings of $28.04 versus $25.65 in assisted living and continuing care retirement communities. The staffing line on a public nursing home profile is being set in a market where the competing setting hires faster and pays more per hour.

**Why it matters:** A family can now open one facility's record and see its fines, its citations by scope and severity, who owns it and what its staffing measures look like, and then see that the sector hiring for those shifts grew 2.1% over the year while home health grew 5.0%. That is the difference between a rating that looks like a fixed judgment and one that reflects a hiring race the facility may be losing. Nursing care facilities employ 1,590.20 thousands of workers; every quality measure in the refreshed files depends on that number holding. For operators, the wage gap of $2.39 an hour between home health and assisted living work is the recruiting problem stated in a single figure.

**Why pitch this now:** The August 2026 employment figures are out, dated 08/01/26, and the CMS nursing home files were refreshed on 08/01/26, so the facility record and the labor market snapshot describe the same month for the first time this quarter. The July 2026 wage series, at $28.04 in home health and $25.65 in assisted living and CCRCs, is current alongside it.

**Angle:** Whether the staffing figure on a nursing home's public profile can mean anything when the workforce that fills it is growing faster in every other setting. Working title: "Where the Shifts Are Going." For skilled nursing operators and staffing directors, and for families weighing a facility against home care.
